title: AI LITERACY
onscreen:
Level 1
Understand AI. Use It Responsibly.
vo: Welcome to AI Literacy, Level 1. This course gives you a practical foundation for understanding AI, using it responsibly, and knowing where human judgment must remain at the center.
build: Title animation only. Keep the screen clean and let the narration introduce the course.

title: What you will learn
onscreen:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:
• Use AI effectively and understand its limitations
• Use AI responsibly and protect sensitive information
• Use basic prompting techniques to guide AI outputs
• Describe what an AI agent is and why its work still needs human review
vo: By the end of this course, you will be able to use AI effectively while understanding its limitations, use AI responsibly while protecting sensitive information, use basic prompting techniques to guide AI outputs, and describe what an AI agent is and why its work still needs human review.
build: Reveal the four outcomes one at a time.

title: The learning journey
onscreen:
1  Understand AI
2  Understand its capabilities and limits
3  See where AI supports work
4  Use AI responsibly
5  Protect information
6  Prompt with purpose
7  Experience an AI agent
8  Demonstrate your judgment
vo: We will move from understanding AI, to understanding what it can and cannot do, to seeing where it can support work. We will then focus on responsible use, information protection, prompting, and a short experience with an AI agent before you complete the assessment.
build: Build the journey as a horizontal path. Highlight the current step as the learner progresses.

title: AWARE is your guide
onscreen:
A  Appreciate AI
W  Weigh the Output
A  Assess the Risk
R  Respond with the Right Prompt
E  Ensure Human Accountability
vo: AWARE is the mental model that connects the course. Appreciate what AI is and what it can do. Weigh the output rather than accepting it automatically. Assess the risks. Respond with a clear prompt. And ensure that human judgment and accountability stay at the center.
build: Animate the five letters in sequence. Do not reteach the framework in the content sections. Reference it only through the AWARE cues listed on slides 6, 19, 30, 32, 34, 39 and 51, the assessment feedback layers, and the closing recap. Use the relevant letter as a small visual cue.

title: Understanding AI
onscreen:
What is AI?
How does generative AI work at a high level?
What language will you hear when people talk about AI?
vo: Let us begin with the foundation: what AI is, what generative AI means, and a few terms you need to recognize.

title: What is Artificial Intelligence?
onscreen:
AI is technology that enables systems to perform tasks that typically require some form of human intelligence.

Recognize patterns  •  Interpret information  •  Generate content  •  Make predictions
vo: Artificial intelligence is technology that enables systems to perform tasks that typically require some form of human intelligence. Depending on the technology, AI can recognize patterns, interpret information, generate content, and make predictions.
build:
Use a central AI node with four surrounding capability cards. Keep the definition visually dominant.
AWARE cue: A (Appreciate AI).

title: AI is a broad field
onscreen:
AI is not one single tool.

Different systems can be designed for different capabilities.
vo: One important point is that AI is a broad field, not one single tool. Different AI systems can be designed for different capabilities. This course focuses on the concepts that apply across AI tools.
build: Show several simple system tiles feeding into one AI umbrella. Avoid naming products.

title: What is Generative AI?
onscreen:
Generative AI creates new content from instructions and context.

TEXT   IMAGES   AUDIO   VIDEO   CODE
vo: Generative AI refers to AI that creates new content. Depending on the system, that content can include text, images, audio, video, or code.
build: Animate the five output types from the center. Keep the definition on screen throughout.

title: What is a Large Language Model?
onscreen: A large language model (LLM) learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses those patterns to generate language.
vo: A large language model, or LLM, learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses those patterns to generate language in response to an instruction. It does this by predicting likely language from what it learned in training, which is why fluent output can still be wrong. The important point for Level 1 is that an LLM generates a response based on learned patterns. That does not mean the response has automatically been checked for accuracy.
build: Show data patterns flowing into a language model and then into a response. Do not imply that the model independently verifies facts.

title: Two terms you will use often
onscreen:
PROMPT
The instruction you give AI

CONTEXT
Information that helps AI interpret the task
vo: A prompt is the instruction you give an AI system. Context is the information that helps the system interpret what you need. You will use both ideas again when we cover prompting.
build: Use two large cards. Reveal prompt first, then context.

title: Three terms to recognize
onscreen:
HALLUCINATION
An inaccurate or unsupported AI output

BIAS
A pattern that can lead to unfair or distorted outcomes

AGENT
An AI system configured to carry out a defined task across multiple steps
vo: A hallucination is an inaccurate or unsupported AI output. Bias can lead to unfair or distorted outcomes. An AI agent is a system configured to carry out a defined task across multiple steps using instructions, context, and available capabilities.
build: Use three cards with a single example icon for each term.

title: What AI Can and Cannot Do
onscreen:
AI can support many kinds of work.
But capability does not equal reliability.
vo: Now that you know what AI is, let us look at a critical distinction: what AI can do is not the same as what AI can reliably do.

title: AI can generate and transform
onscreen:
GENERATE
Create a first draft or new content

TRANSFORM
Rewrite, reformat, translate, or adapt existing content
vo: AI can generate new content and transform existing content. For example, it can create a first draft or adapt information into a different format.
build: Use a before and after visual with two large capability cards.

title: AI can summarize and organize
onscreen:
SUMMARIZE
Condense information into key points

ORGANIZE
Group, structure, or extract information
vo: AI can also summarize information and help organize it. These capabilities can save time, but the resulting output still needs to be reviewed when accuracy matters.
build: Show a long document becoming a concise summary and then a structured list.

title: AI can identify patterns
onscreen:
IDENTIFY PATTERNS
Spot themes, similarities, differences, or recurring information
vo: AI can identify patterns in information. This can be useful for exploring large amounts of content, but pattern recognition does not automatically mean that the interpretation is correct or appropriate.
build: Use a simple visual of repeated items becoming grouped themes.

title: AI cannot guarantee the answer
onscreen:
AI cannot guarantee:
• Accuracy
• Completeness
• Current information
• Fairness
• Appropriate judgment
vo: AI can produce useful output, but it cannot guarantee accuracy, completeness, current information, fairness, or appropriate judgment. Those are areas where human review remains important.
build: Reveal each limitation one at a time. Keep the list short and prominent.

title: Confident does not mean correct
onscreen: CONFIDENT OUTPUT  ≠  CORRECT OUTPUT
vo: One of the most important habits in working with AI is to separate confidence from correctness. An AI response can sound polished and certain while still containing an error.
build:
Make the not-equal symbol the visual focus. Reuse this as a recurring micro-message on slides 30 and 74.
AWARE cue: W (Weigh the Output).

vo:

title: AI at Work
onscreen:
Think  •  Create  •  Understand  •  Explore

AI supports the work. People own the work.
vo: AI can support work in many ways. At Level 1, the goal is not to teach specific workflows. It is to understand the role AI can play and the role people must continue to play.

title: AI can help you think and create
onscreen:
THINK
Brainstorm ideas and options

CREATE
Draft or generate content
vo: AI can support thinking by helping you brainstorm ideas and options. It can also support creation by producing a starting draft or alternative versions.
build: Use two large cards with light motion from idea to draft.

title: AI can help you understand and explore
onscreen:
UNDERSTAND
Summarize, explain, or clarify information

EXPLORE
Look across information for themes, patterns, or questions
vo: AI can help you understand information by summarizing, explaining, or clarifying it. It can also help you explore themes, patterns, or questions in information.
build: Use document and magnifying-glass style editable shapes.

title: AI is an assistant, not the owner
onscreen:
AI can suggest, generate, organize, and assist.

The person still provides context, judgment, verification, and decisions.
vo: The safest way to think about AI at work is as an assistant, not the owner of the work. AI can suggest, generate, organize, and assist. People provide the context, judgment, verification, and decisions. This matters most when work affects people, business decisions, or important outcomes, so people remain responsible for evaluating the output and making the decision.
build: Use a simple two-column visual: AI assists on the left, human owns the work on the right. Then animate the handoff from AI output to human review and decision.

title: Responsible AI
onscreen:
Pause before you trust the output.

Check accuracy. Consider fairness. Respect intellectual property. Review use. Keep human accountability.
vo: Responsible AI is about how we use AI, not just what AI can produce. We will focus on accuracy, fairness, intellectual property, appropriate use, and accountability.

title: Accuracy: pause, check, verify
onscreen:
PAUSE
Do not accept the output automatically

CHECK
Identify claims that matter

VERIFY
Use an appropriate reliable source

An output can be fluent and polished and still be wrong. If the consequence matters, verify.
vo: When accuracy matters, pause before using the output. Check the claims that matter and verify them using an appropriate reliable source. AI systems can produce inaccurate or unsupported information, sometimes called hallucinations. Do not judge accuracy by how polished the answer sounds.
build:
Build the three steps as a simple horizontal process. Show a polished answer card with a subtle warning marker. Avoid scary imagery.
AWARE cue: W (Weigh the Output).

title: Practice: spot the claims to verify
onscreen:
An AI draft says (fictional example):

Our travel policy was updated in March 2022. It allows up to $75 per day for meals, as stated in Section 4.2 of the handbook.

Select every claim you would verify.
vo: Here is a short AI-generated answer. It sounds polished, but not every detail can be trusted. Select the claims you would verify before using it.
build:

CORRECT: Specific dates, amounts, and references are exactly the details AI can get wrong, so all three should be checked against the official source. INCORRECT: Look again. Any specific date, number, or reference needs checking, however polished the answer sounds. Allow one retry.
AWARE cue: W (Weigh the Output).

title: Bias and fairness
onscreen:
ASK
Could this output disadvantage someone?

REVIEW
Pay closer attention when people may be affected.
vo: AI can reflect patterns or biases present in the information used to develop or operate a system. When people may be affected, review the output for fairness and apply human judgment.
build:
Use a balance visual with a question prompt. Keep the wording neutral and practical.
AWARE cue: A (Assess the Risk).

title: Copyright and intellectual property
onscreen:
Before you use or share AI-generated content:

CHECK  Does it copy or closely resemble protected material?
REVIEW  Who owns it, and what permissions apply?
CONFIRM  Does your organization allow this use?
vo: AI-generated or transformed content is not automatically free to use. Consider ownership, permissions, copyright, intellectual property requirements, and your organization's expectations before using or sharing content. AI output can resemble existing protected material, and ownership of AI-generated content can vary by location, so follow your organization's guidance.
build: Use three editable check cards. Avoid legal claims beyond the source material.

title: When AI should not be the decision-maker
onscreen:
Do not delegate sensitive decisions or accountability to AI.

Especially when decisions affect people or carry significant consequences.

AI can assist. Humans remain accountable.
vo: There are situations where AI should support the process rather than make the decision. Do not delegate sensitive decisions or accountability to AI, especially when people may be affected or consequences are significant. In many places, decisions about employees and candidates are also covered by laws and policies that require human oversight. This is the core principle of the course: AI can assist, but humans remain accountable for how outputs are reviewed, used, and acted upon. Where your organization expects it, be open about when AI was used.
build:
Use a decision gate visual. Close with AI can assist. Humans remain accountable. as a strong visual statement, and reuse the phrase at the end of the course.
AWARE cue: E (Ensure Human Accountability).

title: Data, Privacy and Security
onscreen: Before you share information with an AI tool, stop and assess the information, the tool, and your permission to use it.
vo: Responsible AI also means protecting information. Depending on the tool and its settings, information you enter may be stored, reviewed, or used to improve the tool. Before you enter information into an AI tool, consider what the information is, who owns it, whether the tool is approved, and whether you are permitted to use it.

title: Think before you share
onscreen:
1  What information is it?
2  Who owns it?
3  Is the tool approved?
4  Am I permitted to use it?
vo: Use four questions before sharing information with an AI tool. What information is it? Who owns it? Is the tool approved? And am I permitted to use it?
build:

AWARE cue: A (Assess the Risk).

title: Information to protect
onscreen:
CONFIDENTIAL
SENSITIVE
EMPLOYEE
CANDIDATE
PERSONAL
CLIENT
PROPRIETARY
CREDENTIALS
vo: Protect confidential, sensitive, employee, candidate, personal, client, and proprietary information, as well as login credentials. The ability of a tool to process information does not mean you are permitted to share that information with it.

title: Use approved tools
onscreen:
APPROVED TOOL
+
PERMISSION
+
POLICY REQUIREMENTS
vo: Use approved AI tools and follow organizational policies and permissions. Unapproved tools may not meet your organization's security requirements. If you are unsure whether information may be used with a tool, stop and check the applicable requirement before proceeding.
build: Use a three-part gate visual. Do not name internal tools unless the organization has approved them for the audience.

title: Protect the information throughout the process
onscreen:
Before input  →  During use  →  Before sharing output

Protect information at every stage.
vo: Information protection does not stop when you enter the prompt. Consider the information before input, during use, and again before sharing the output. During use, stay within approved tools and share only what the task needs.

title: Prompting Fundamentals
onscreen: A useful prompt gives AI enough information to interpret what you need.
vo: Once you know how AI works at a high level and how to use it responsibly, the next step is giving clear instructions. Prompting is simply communicating what you need from the system.

title: Start with context
onscreen:
CONTEXT
What does AI need to know to interpret the situation?
vo: Context gives AI the information it needs to interpret the situation. Think about the background, source information, or relevant details that shape the task.
build: Reveal the single prompt element, then move to the next. Keep the visual pattern consistent.

title: Define the task
onscreen:
TASK
What exactly do you want AI to do?
vo: State the task clearly. Tell AI what you want it to produce, change, summarize, compare, or organize.
build: Reveal the single prompt element, then move to the next. Keep the visual pattern consistent.

title: Specify the audience
onscreen:
AUDIENCE
Who is the output for?
vo: Tell AI who will use or read the output. Audience can influence language, detail, tone, and emphasis.
build: Reveal the single prompt element, then move to the next. Keep the visual pattern consistent.

title: Describe the output
onscreen:
OUTPUT
What should the result look like?
vo: Describe the result you want. You can specify format, structure, or other output expectations.
build: Reveal the single prompt element, then move to the next. Keep the visual pattern consistent.

title: Add constraints
onscreen:
CONSTRAINTS
What boundaries should AI follow?
vo: Add useful boundaries such as length, deadline, tone, required elements, or information that must be included or excluded.
build: Reveal the single prompt element, then move to the next. Keep the visual pattern consistent.

title: Put the pieces together
onscreen:
CONTEXT + TASK + AUDIENCE + OUTPUT + CONSTRAINTS

A clearer instruction gives AI a clearer target. Review the result, then refine.
vo: The five fundamentals work together. Context, task, audience, output, and constraints give AI a clearer target. You do not need advanced prompting techniques for this level. After you get a response, review it and refine your prompt if needed.
build:
Animate each element into one prompt structure.
AWARE cue: R (Respond with the Right Prompt).

title: AI Agents and Atlas Experience
onscreen: From a single response to a defined task
vo: You now have the foundation to understand what an AI agent is. In this section, you will see the difference between a chatbot and an agent and then experience a simple agent scenario in Atlas.

title: What is an AI agent?
onscreen:
An AI agent is an AI system configured to carry out a defined task across multiple steps using:

INSTRUCTIONS  +  CONTEXT  +  AVAILABLE CAPABILITIES
vo: At a high level, an AI agent is an AI system configured to carry out a defined task across multiple steps using instructions, context, and available capabilities. An agent can work through a defined task or sequence rather than simply returning one response. It can use tools to take actions, which is why its work still needs review.
build: Use a three-input model flowing into a defined task. Keep this conceptual.

title: Chatbot versus AI agent
onscreen:
CHATBOT
You ask → AI responds

AGENT
You define a task → Agent works through it
vo: A chatbot typically responds to the request you make. An agent can be configured around a defined task and work through that task using its instructions, context, and capabilities. The difference is not the interface. An agent is set up to work through several steps toward a goal, often using tools, while a chatbot usually answers one request at a time.
build: Use two lanes. Animate the chatbot response as one step and the agent task as a short sequence.
